articles.title_orig: Sanctioned Russian military aircraft lands at Ben-Gurion Airport in Israel
articles.title_zh: Sanctioned Russian military aircraft lands at Ben-Gurion Airport in Israel
articles.content_orig:
A Russian military transport aircraft carrying a senior delegation led by the head of Russia’s military intelligence agency landed at Ben-Gurion Airport on Saturday evening in an unusual visit, two sources familiar with the matter told The Jerusalem Post .
The delegation, which met senior Israeli defense officials, was headed by Admiral Igor Kostyukov, chief of the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation, commonly known as the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency.
The purpose of the visit and the subjects discussed during the delegation’s meetings in Israel remain unclear, but the unusual landing of a Russian military aircraft in Israel comes amid heightened regional tensions and ongoing uncertainty over the possibility of renewed military confrontation between the US, Israel and Iran.
The Russian aircraft departed Israel and headed to Abu Dhabi.
The Russian delegation, including Kostyukov, will participate in the Russian-Ukrainian negotiations under US mediation scheduled for Tuesday-Wednesday.
A jet operated by the Russian Defense Ministry landed in Israel's Ben-Gurion Airport on Sunday evening, flight-tracking data from FlightRadar24 showed.
The Tupolev Tu-154M, which departed from a military base near Moscow , has been on the US sanctions list since 2023.
The Chkalovsky Air Base from which the flight originated is the primary operational hub for the Russian Defense Ministry, which manages VIP transport and government missions for high-ranking military officials and official delegations.
The flight path went over the Black Sea and through Turkish airspace before entering Israel from the Mediterranean. The plane circled over Israel before landing at Ben-Gurion Airport at about 7 p.m.
Flightradar24 data showed that in the past week, the aircraft has remained in Moscow since arriving from Novosibirsk on November 2.
The aircraft belongs to the 223rd Flight Unit of the Russian Defense Ministry, itself a sanctioned entity, as the US State Department accused the unit of transporting personnel and equipment belonging to the Wagner mercenary group to countries where Wagner operated.
The aircraft was listed under Executive Order 14024, which authorizes sanctions targeting Russia's harmful foreign activities, including those connected to its war against Ukraine.
As part of the May 19, 2023, action, the US identified 37 aircraft associated with the unit as blocked property, including RA-85042.
When approached by The Jerusalem Post , the Russian Embassy in Israel declined to comment on who was in the aircraft or why they were in Israel.
Additionally, the IDF declined the Post's request for comment.
The Post also reached out to several US government bodies for comment.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s affair with alleged Chinese spy puts Nvidia’s China ambitions under scrutiny
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 6% on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying "allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report , external .
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.
After the investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Huang to continue leading the firm.
US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".
However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (Â£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.
While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened on a positive note on Monday after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.
But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so central to the AI industry.
"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.
Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.
Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but Huang decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.
A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.
Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.
He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.
By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.
Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."
The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.
Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.
What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy
Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.
Additional reporter by Samira Hussain, North America business correspondent.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Opens 700 Points Higher, Nvidia Stock Slides After Jensen Huang Apologizes for Affair
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Opens 700 Points Higher, Nvidia Stock Slides After Jensen Huang Apologizes for Affair
articles.content_orig:
CEO reportedly ‌had close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing
Nvidia said ⁠on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The New York Times reported in ​October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”
Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.
Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Huang fully ‌supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Axios reported on ​Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full ⁠responsibility for his actions.
“I was unfaithful to my ​wife. My ​actions hurt her ​and our children. There is no excuse ​for what ‌I did,” ​Huang said ​in the draft email also seen by Reuters.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.
The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump’s delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China’s president.
Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.
Nick Robins-Early and Blake Montgomery contributed reporting

articles.title_zh: Nvidia cracks down on overseas cloud AI GPU rentals for China — partners face 51% non-Chinese quota as black market B300 rack prices surge to $2.8 million
articles.content_orig:

Nvidia-based compute is getting scarce and expensive for Chinese AI labs on both of their main routes, buying export-compliant cards and renting abroad, and the Financial Times reports that Nvidia’s own crackdowns are part of the reason. Nvidia has told cloud partners worldwide that at least 51% of their services must go to non-Chinese firms, while Chinese companies have bought more than 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation cards this year to cover the shortfall. Meanwhile, a B300 rack that sells for about $600,000 internationally reportedly fetched $2.8 million in China last month.
Chinese customers have ordered more than 6 million of Nvidia’s export-compliant RTX Pro 5500 cards. That is at least twice the 3 million that the company could reportedly manufacture in 2027. One source told CNBC that it was proposed that Moonshot pay 30% to 50% more upfront, in comparison to a non-Chinese entity.
Many Chinese groups have relied on overseas leases for advanced AI work, which can include model training, and these tech groups have been the biggest clients for data centers in Southeast Asia. Data centers unable to find non-Chinese clients could be forced to pull back supply, and it’s “difficult to find enough non-Chinese clients outside the US,” one Singapore-based group told the FT . While Nvidia hasn’t confirmed or denied its new rule, implementing it would ease criticism from U.S. lawmakers just as Chinese demand is growing.
What Nvidia told partners has come through verbal instructions, via sales and regional teams, and applies globally rather than just in Asia. Existing deals and leases are not changed, but new ones must comply. Nvidia’s whitelist more than halved its authorized Asian buyer count, which encouraged more Chinese groups to lease over other options, including smuggling. On top of this, Fleet Intelligence tracking is now required for Southeast Asian providers that want to become Nvidia Cloud Partners. All of these combined — whitelist, cap, and tracking — may act to alleviate U.S. concerns.
Among companies that have moved to renting, Moonshot has held discussions to rent capacity from neoclouds that host in Europe with Nvidia GPUs. Specifically, it’s looking for Nvidia Blackwell systems, which export controls bar from China; one source said the talks covered clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs in Europe. These clusters would handle inference, serving models to end users, and the European talks for them happened after the White House said Moonshot accessed Blackwell chips through a facility in Thailand . The firm has been fervent about its intentions to secure more compute.
Moonshot isn't the only Chinese company looking to secure Nvidia chips for AI training. Tencent has a deal with Oracle to lease 100,000 GPUs in Southeast Asian data centers. ByteDance and Alibaba are also pursuing similar long-term leases, and most of these overseas data centers run chips like the forbidden B300. MiniMax, like Moonshot, also leases significant compute both at home and abroad.
The big reason is that domestic AI chip supply is simply not up to the task, although not for a lack of trying. Huawei is expected to hit 1.6 million chips this year, with about 1 million from Alibaba and Baidu, and 300,000 from Cambricon. Total supply this year will be up to 3.5 million, including about 1 million made overseas, against a demand that far exceeds 5 million. That number could more than double next year.
Part of the problem is that the export-compliant cards Chinese firms have been buying , mostly the RTX Pro 6000D, RTX Pro 5000, and RTX 5090, are mostly useful for simpler work such as prefill. Even so, the discontinued 6000D’s pricing in China has reportedly doubled. Huawei’s Ascend 910C outperforms them in most areas, but these lower-end options are still coveted, partly because of a preference for CUDA over Huawei’s CANN. Nvidia’s programming platform is supported by most AI frameworks and libraries, and much in-house code is optimized for it.
Then there’s the RTX Pro 5500 , with 84GB of GDDR7 with ECC and 1,398 GB/s of memory bandwidth. The card runs on a full PCIe Gen 5 x16 interface, draws up to 600 W, and can be split into up to two MIG instances. That still leaves it well short of a B300, which has about 3.4 times the memory and 5.7 times the bandwidth, plus NVLink, which the 5500 lacks.
Export-compliant; samples in December, deliveries from Q1 2027
Licensed by the U.S. case by case; Beijing withholding approval for large-scale imports
Banned for sale to China; rented abroad
Indicated orders from China are not precise, but the total of over six million includes more than three million from ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent. The big three ordered at about $11,400 each, for a total sticker price over $35 billion. This is difficult to fill when there may be fewer than three million produced next year, and partners might only actually get 5% to 10% of the original ask. Starting in 2027, much of Nvidia’s TSMC capacity may shift to Rubin, taking more production, while the RTX Pro 5500’s early samples are due in December.
On the legal side, it’s currently easier to rent than to own as current U.S. law does not give regulators broad authority over overseas cloud access. The Remote Access Security Act (RASA), which would extend U.S. export controls to that area, has sailed through the House but has not yet passed the Senate. Those directly affected — neoclouds and related financiers — price in a possible ban regardless, which drives the upfront premium.
China’s side is not completely clean, either, with about 600,000 H200s reportedly stuck in storage in Hong Kong awaiting shipment to the mainland. Beijing is withholding approvals for large-volume imports such as this. Only relatively small quantities have come in during recent months, for some big internet companies, with others coming through intermediaries and indirect routes in small quantities. The price: over $900,000 for an eight-card H200 server in China at the end of last month, about 3x the cost a year ago. This is despite the fact that H200 sales are already under U.S. license.
The first test that will show how many cards will actually land occurs in Q1 2027, when the RTX Pro 5500 is expected in commercial deliveries. For rentals, whether or not the Remote Access Security Act is a factor depends on a Senate vote, which is not yet scheduled. Nvidia’s Q3 results come in soon, on Nov. 17, which could bring some illumination.
With CEO Jensen Huang under scrutiny lately over reports that he was targeted by an alleged Chinese spy , which Nvidia’s board is now investigating, he’s going to feel the heat even more just a day later, when lawmakers have asked him to attend a closed-door briefing. He’s been pushing for laxer controls and more access, so the assumed 51% rule will also be put to the test.
Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title_orig: The two East German officials who accidentally brought down the Berlin Wall
articles.title_zh: The two East German officials who accidentally brought down the Berlin Wall
articles.content_orig:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called for the protection of freedom and democracy in Germany and Europe on the 37th anniversary of the fall of the Berlin Wall.
In a post on Monday on X, Merz recalled the three pivotal events of November 9 in German history: the proclamation of the republic in 1918, the Nazi pogroms of 1938 against Jews, and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.
"November 9 stands for the darkest and happiest hours of our history: for anti-Semitism and persecution, for the beginning of democracy and the fall of the wall," Merz said.
Merz added: "Freedom and democracy are never a given. Let us protect them - in Germany and Europe."
November 9 holds a unique place in Germany's collective memory.
In 1918, the abdication of Kaiser Wilhelm II paved the way for the proclamation of the republic; in 1938, the Nazi regime unleashed nationwide attacks that marked the start of the systematic killing of Jews and a sharp increase in their persecution; and in 1989, the fall of the Berlin Wall signalled the end of Germany's division and the start of reunification.
Later on Monday, Merz will attend a ceremony in Munich marking the 20th anniversary of the establishment of the Ohel Jakob synagogue, alongside Bavarian premier Markus Söder and the president of the Bavarian state parliament, Ilse Aigner.
Aigner is widely expected to be nominated to succeed outgoing federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, potentially becoming the first woman to serve as German president.

articles.title_orig: Trump talked with Fed chief, but there’s no record of it on Warsh’s calendar
articles.title_zh: Trump talked with Fed chief, but there’s no record of it on Warsh’s calendar
articles.content_orig:
Tom Boggioni is a writer, born, raised and living in San Diego — where he attended San Diego State University. Prior to writing for Raw Story, he wrote for FireDogLake, blogged as TBogg, and worked in banking, marketing and construction.
Democrats want answers from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh , demanding to know whether he is hiding secret conversations with Donald Trump .
The president says he and Warsh have talked. Warsh’s official records say they haven’t. And the Fed chair isn’t explaining the gap, the Washington Post reported.
On Friday, the Fed released Warsh’s September calendar, and once again, Trump’s name doesn’t appear. That makes "five months in a row," every month since Warsh took over in May, with no logged contact with the president. It comes despite a request this summer from Senate Democrats that he include any such conversations.
According to the Post, " The calendars are one of the few windows into how often a president reaches the official who leads the central bank’s decisions on interest rates , and previous Fed chairs have recorded interactions with presidents there. The Fed is designed to operate independently of the White House , setting rates based on its own best assessment of the economy rather than short-term political pressure."
On Sept. 16, the same day Warsh and his colleagues raised rates a quarter point against Trump’s wishes, the president told reporters he had weighed in on Warsh’s vote.
“I talked to Kevin, and I said, ‘You might as well vote with the board ’cause it’s not gonna matter,’” Trump said, noting that Warsh lacked the votes to change the outcome.
When a reporter asked if he had tried to sway Warsh, Trump said he hadn’t. “No, I didn’t convince him. No, I said, ‘Do what you want,’” he said, adding that he wanted Warsh “to be independent.”
Neither side has cleared it up, the report notes. The White House has refused to say when that conversation took place, and Warsh won’t confirm it ever happened.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) and three other Democratic senators wrote to Warsh in August, asking him to state in writing whether he had spoken with Trump and to correct his calendars if so. Van Hollen’s office told the Post on Friday that Warsh never replied.
“It’s clear neither Warsh nor Trump give a damn about transparency to the American people,” Van Hollen said. “Under a Democratic majority in Congress, we will continue pushing for that much-needed transparency.”

articles.title_orig: US-led peace talks for Russia and Ukraine will look at security guarantees for both sides
articles.title_zh: US-led peace talks for Russia and Ukraine will look at security guarantees for both sides
articles.content_orig:
US secretary of state says some progress made on what security infrastructure could look like in Ukraine and Europe after the war. What we know on day 1,720
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said some progress had been made on what the “security infrastructure” of Ukraine and Europe could look like after the war with Russia, adding that talks this week could lead to further advances. Rubio’s comments on Sunday, ahead of his travel to Paris for talks with G7 foreign ministers, come as Russia-Ukraine negotiations under US mediation have been set for Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump’s son-in-law, will represent the US in Abu Dhabi.
In an interview ‌with CBS’s “60 Minutes” broadcast on Sunday, Trump said he believed the war would end ‌soon and suggested Ukraine could emerge from a settlement with altered borders. “I think we’re gonna have it done, and I think it’s gonna happen and they’re gonna end up with a little bit different shape Ukraine,” Trump said. Asked whether Russian president Vladimir Putin was stringing him along, Trump replied: “Oh, I don’t think so.”
On Sunday, Rubio said the whole time the US had been talking about Russia and Ukraine, “the one thing that’s repeatedly come up is the need for security guarantees” and what they would look like in Ukraine, and on the European continent. “I think that’s what the president’s alluding to – is that there’s been some advances made in what that architecture could look like post-conflict.”
French ⁠Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Europe would be well represented at the talks. “France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in ⁠these discussions,” Barrot told French radio station RTL. “I can’t ​tell you yet who will be ‌representing France on this ‌occasion, but France will certainly be there,” he added.
A Russian drone has struck emergency workers on rescue missions in southern Ukraine. Authorities say the attack on Sunday hit a former school and nearby shelter in the village of Komyshuvakha, previously targeted by Russian bombs. Ukraine said last Monday’s attack killed at least 55 people. No injuries were reported in Sunday’s strike but rescue equipment was damaged. About 50 people remain missing.
Power has been restored to the Russian-controlled ⁠Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine, hours after the plant lost its external electricity ⁠supply and had ⁠to ​use backup generators for reactor cooling, the UN’s nuclear watchdog said on Sunday. Zaporizhzhia, which does ⁠not produce electricity but needs power supplied by two external links to keep nuclear fuel cool, lost ⁠its off-site electricity supply earlier on Sunday after the Ferosplavna power ​line disconnected. The International Atomic ‌Energy Agency said the cause and location of the disconnection were unknown. The loss of power was the plant’s 27th such incident since the beginning of the conflict.
Russia said ⁠on Sunday overnight strikes by its forces had hit three cargo vessels ⁠that were carrying military ⁠goods ​for Ukraine and two electricity substations , which it said supplied power to ⁠the Ukrainian defence industry, Reuters reports. Russia’s defence ministry said Russian forces had struck a container ship delivering ⁠weapons and military equipment to the Black Sea ​port of Odesa, ‌and another in ‌the port of Chornomorsk, which is in the same ‌southwestern region of Ukraine. According to the ministry, the second container ship had delivered dual-use cargo to Ukraine. It said a third vessel, a dry cargo ship hit south-west of Odesa, ‌was carrying weapons and military equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces.
Moldova on Sunday launched a new power line connecting the country to neighbouring Romania and the European grid, to reduce its reliance on Russian energy . “For decades, Moscow used energy to blackmail us,” President Maia Sandu wrote on X. “No more. Moldova buys zero Russian gas.” Achieving energy security is a priority for the former Soviet republic of 2.6 million people, which has faced difficulties since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title_orig: Russia-Ukraine war: Nine Zimbabweans caught trying to leave South Africa to join conflict
articles.title_zh: Russia-Ukraine war: Nine Zimbabweans caught trying to leave South Africa to join conflict
articles.content_orig:
Nine Zimbabweans have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and the Ukraine, police say.
The group, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in and around Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team on Sunday evening.
They were caught as they were "preparing to board flights out of the country", authorities added, but their final destination is unclear.
They have been charged with contravening South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which outlaws mercenary activity without government permission.
Police said five people were arrested at South Africa's biggest airport, OR Tambo, and another four at a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team that involved Interpol.
All nine later appeared in court, according to state prosecutors.
The police statement added that the involvement of Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies indicated that the suspects had also allegedly violated laws in their respective home countries, prompting cooperation with South African authorities.
They have also not said whether the group allegedly intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine nor provided details of the organisations allegedly involved in facilitating their travel.
Citizens of several African countries, including Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, have gone to fight for Russia in Ukraine - some they had been duped and had not realised where they were going.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.
Kenya at the time estimated that 252 citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia. In March, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue.
He said at the time that an agreement had been reached to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.
In March, Zimbabwe said that 15 of its nationals had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine, with more than 60 still trapped on the frontlines.
The previous month, South Africa secured the return of 17 South Africans who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.
In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.
Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.

articles.title_zh: Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines
articles.content_orig:

AI’s power crunch has become so acute that Anthropic, a company that has generally avoided buying physical infrastructure, is spending $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines.
The AI company, which is planning to go public this year, is buying Caterpillar generators that equipment supplier OnePWR had originally ordered, according to a Financial Times report . The generators are capable of producing up to 1.7 gigawatts of electricity.
Historically, Anthropic has preferred to rent rather than buy. The company disclosed in its S-1 filing in May that it is paying SpaceX subsidiary xAI $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 to use xAI’s computing power.
“We expect to enter into additional similar services contracts,” Anthropic stated in the filing, meaning more deals to rent computing power.
But as demand for compute ramps up, the market for power has also grown increasingly uncertain, which may have forced its hand. The backlog for natural gas turbines stretches into the early 2030s, and queues to connect to the electrical grid can be just as long.
Anthropic’s purchase looks like a last resort.
According to the report, OnePWR ordered the turbines a couple years ago, but couldn’t find financing to complete the purchase. Anthropic had planned to buy them from OnePWR but instead went directly to Caterpillar, the manufacturer.
It’s not clear why OnePWR was unable to secure financing despite Anthropic’s apparent interest as a customer. Whatever the case, Anthropic likely wanted to keep the generating capacity to itself rather than give a competitor an opportunity to snap it up.
AI companies have been ramping up their purchases of natural gas equipment and supplies in recent years. Google , Amazon , Microsoft , and Meta have all announced plans to build massive natural gas power plants to power their data centers on site, rather than drawing from the public grid.
The binge has given a second wind to fracking , the drilling method used to extract natural gas from underground rock. And if the buildout proceeds as planned, U.S. data centers alone could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035. The reliance on natural gas also exposes hyperscalers to price fluctuations. One analyst expects that prices could more than triple by the end of the decade in some markets. If that happens, Anthropic might have a serious case of buyer’s remorse.

articles.title_orig: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.title_zh: France accuses Iran of supermarket fridge hacking
articles.content_orig:
France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind cyber-attacks that raised the temperatures of supermarket fridges and freezers across the country last month.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression", adding those who were responsible would be hit with sanctions "at the European level".
Iran is yet to respond to Barrot's allegations.
The cyber-attack last month saw fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets across France heated up, which spoilt fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Then last week, dozens of supermarkets across several other European countries were also impacted by a cyber-attack that targeted fridges and freezers. It is not known if the instances are linked.
Barrot said the attack on France's supermarkets "marks the first large-scale cyber-attack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people".
He said the government had summoned the Iranian ambassador to Paris to "lodge a very strong protest against this extremely grave act".
France will take "any other necessary and proportionate measures" to respond to the incident and "deter anyone who might seek to repeat it", Barrot added.
Separately on Monday, the Paris prosecutor said an investigation had been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit associated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as well as his two deputies.
Laure Beccuau named the unit as Shahid Kaveh, which she said had an affiliation with the electronic and cyber centre of the IRGC.
Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.
On 11 October, hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units used in many of France's supermarkets.
More than 100 of Coopérative U's supermarkets were hit, as well as 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand. In some stores, temperatures of the fridges reportedly rose to 50C (120F) overnight.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Earlier this month a second wave of hacks took place, hitting more than 100 stores across Europe.
Supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in countries including Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Separately in August a small number of US military bases had fridges mysteriously malfunction, spoiling food. This incident is also being investigated as deliberate cyber-attacks, Reuters news agency has reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Since the waves of attacks on freezers, experts have been speculating which hacking groups could be responsible, with Iran being on a list of potential suspects.
In spite of a pair of Russian-aligned hacktivist groups claiming they were responsible on Wednesday, few believed them.
The French government has not said how it reached the conclusion that Iran was responsible, and attribution of cyber attacks is extremely hard as hackers are able to hide their locations.

articles.title_orig: Poundland unable to buy new stock as fears over collapse grow
articles.title_zh: Poundland unable to buy new stock as fears over collapse grow
articles.content_orig:
Poundland is unable to buy new stock to fill its shelves after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.
The discount chain is on the brink of collapse with one insider describing it as "running on fumes". It has until Thursday to secure a rescue deal.
About £50m has been frozen by its American owner Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning its 600 shops are running out of stock.
Pressure is building on Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for £1 last June, after the owner rejected a takeover bid that could have saved the thousands of jobs currently at risk. Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.
Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until Thursday.
Access to funds was limited because of a tension between Gordon Brothers' dual role as both creditor and shareholder, a source said, but added they expected a relaxation of funds in the next two days.
Last week, Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4% last week, which included Halloween, but said this was £1.5m ahead of budget.
He said the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where the business made losses of £68m.
The latest annual accounts have yet to be audited.
However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture of the business, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".
It said it had provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.
It has also made £18m, from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.
On Wednesday, executives from Gordon Brothers will appear before the Business Select Committee with MPs probing whether they are genuinely pursuing a solvent rescue of the business, which has 11,000 employees, and whether every realistic step is being taken to protect jobs and stores.
The session is being held in private given commercially sensitive discussions are still under way with bidders.
On Thursday, the 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended.
If not, Poundland is set to collapse into administration and could be broken up.
A source familiar with the sales process said London-based Xyra Group was making "significant progress" in its last minute bid to buy Poundland and could now be the front runner.
An extension of Thursday's deadline now seems an increasingly likely scenario. But such a case would be difficult to put forward if Gordon Brothers continues to block funding.
One observer remarked "if Gordon Brothers is going in front of that committee, you don't want to be giving the message we're pulling up the drawbridge".
Even if a deal is agreed to sell the business as a whole, there is no guarantee a new owner would not reduce the number of stores, but suppliers to Poundland would prefer that outcome to hundreds of sites being sold off to other retailers.
There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up stores which could mean continuing employment for many workers.
The central issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland trading as a national chain.

articles.title_orig: Carney Recruits Bridgewater Co-CIO to Run Canada Sovereign Wealth Fund
articles.title_zh: Carney Recruits Bridgewater Co-CIO to Run Canada Sovereign Wealth Fund
articles.content_orig:
A top executive at one of the world's largest hedge funds is leaving her job in the U.S. to become the CEO of one of the Carney government's hallmark projects.
On Monday, the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) announced that Karen Karniol-Tambour will become the CEO of Canada's nascent sovereign wealth fund.
A news release from the PMO said Karniol-Tambour has Canadian citizenship, though public records indicate she was born in Israel and has spent her professional career in the United States.
Her LinkedIn page says she has been at Bridgewater Associates for more than 20 years and rose to be co-chief investment officer. She graduated from Princeton University in 2006.
Carney's bet on economic growth — and the risks that come with it
Mark Carney's quiet revolution rests on investment and affordability
The financial magazine Barron's has named Karniol-Tambour in its list of the 100 most influential women in U.S. finance for the last seven years. She was also featured by Forbes .
At the helm of the new sovereign wealth fund, she will be tasked with identifying and investing in domestic projects with the goal of generating returns for investors and reinvesting them in new Canadian projects.
The federal government announced plans to create the fund, which it is calling the Canada Strong Fund, last spring. It has earmarked $25 billion in seed funding and committed to putting commercial asset revenue into the fund. Its goal is to finance "nation-building" projects while allowing Canadians to benefit from the returns.
The fund will also include a "retail" element for ordinary Canadians to be able to buy in directly . Last week's federal budget said those investments will take the form of notes similar to savings bonds, but details on when or how that will roll out haven't been announced.
"Under Ms. Karniol-Tambour’s leadership, the Canada Strong Fund will be professionally managed, operating at arm's length from the government, with its own board of directors," said the Prime Minister's Office.
"Together, the fund and its retail offering will create a new model of Canadian ownership, helping build national wealth while ensuring more Canadians share in the benefits of economic growth."
Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title_orig: Silicon Valley and Trump rally behind Nvidia CEO after his affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.title_zh: Silicon Valley and Trump rally behind Nvidia CEO after his affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk and other finance moguls defend Jensen Huang after he admitted to the affair in an email to employees
Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish
Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
“I have not ​spoken to him about it,” Trump told reporters on Sunday. “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on. I’m sure, I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job”.
“I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it,” Trump later added, saying he believed that Huang would and should stay on as CEO.
Huang’s defenders framed his affair as a personal lapse in judgment rather than evidence of treachery against the United States, which has imposed strict limits on what chips Nvidia can sell to China.
Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, admitted in an email to employees on Sunday that he had an affair and that he would cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s board of directors put out a statement the same day that the company was launching a probe regarding reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
The chip mogul is alleged to have had a relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman that US intelligence services suspect of spying for the Chinese government, according to The New York Times . Trump was reportedly briefed on the relationship last year, the Times reported, but took no action. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are unrelated, with the latter being one of the world’s richest men and CEO of Nvidia, worth more than $4tn, for the past 33 years.
US intelligence agencies believe Alice Huang, acting on behalf of Beijing, pushed Jensen Huang to lobby Trump for relaxed export controls on Nvidia’s sales in China, which he has done multiple times publicly. Nvidia said in a statement that neither trade secrets nor US national security had been compromised.
The affair and alleged intelligence operation involving Huang could have far reaching implications for Nvidia and the tech industry, which are already enduring a period of high market volatility . Huang’s leadership of Nvidia, which is deeply financially intertwined with other leading tech companies like OpenAI, has long been viewed as crucial to the company’s success and stability.
As news of the scandal broke over the weekend, Musk and prominent investors shared their support of Huang. Musk posted “I agree” in response to prominent venture capitalist Shaun Maguire’s defense of Huang. Maguire argued the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”.
“Two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” Maguire posted. He stated the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”.
“Let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op,” Maguire added in a separate post.
Bill Ackman , the US hedge fund manager and pro-Trump billionaire, meanwhile, suggested that Huang is “human” and deserves public support over the affair.
“He is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes,” Ackman posted. “He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family. Onward.”
Ackman followed up with another post later clarifying that he wasn’t suggesting Huang “gets a free pass” but that he was “hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security”.

articles.title_zh: Oil Falls on Unconfirmed Report That Iran Eased Hormuz Demands
articles.content_orig:
Brent crude futures hit their lowest since early September on Monday ​after U.S. President Donald Trump ​downplayed the likelihood of ​renewed strikes on Iran, though attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz kept supply concerns in focus.
Trump said on Sunday that he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as ⁠long ‌as talks to end the conflict progressed, even as both ⁠countries reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude futures were down $5.05, or 5.2%, to $93.27 a barrel, having slid as low as $93.21 a barrel earlier. U.S. West Texas ‌Intermediate lost $4.12, or 4.5%, to $86.71.
The Brent benchmark plunged by 16% last week to touch a two-month low of $93.22, its steepest weekly decline since the start ​of the Covid-19 pandemic.
"Oil continues to trade lower on hopes of a U.S.-Iran peace deal rather than concrete signs of progress," said Saxo Bank analyst Ole Hansen, adding that Trump's latest comments that fresh strikes on Iran are highly unlikely have ⁠increased downward pressure on prices.
UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said: "Weakness in the physical market, supported by still-elevated flows out of ‌the Middle East, is one factor weighing on prices."
Dated Brent, ‌used to price cargoes around the world, has weakened to a discount to the nearby Brent futures contract, Morgan Stanley said in a report on Monday, highlighting weakness in the physical market.
Trump had hinted at ⁠a resumption of attacks on Iran after last week's U.S. midterm elections, but there ⁠has been no sign of a large-scale U.S. military operation. Iran has said ⁠it would respond by striking U.S. and Israeli targets.
Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade, called Trump's comments "more measured" but said the market is still ​waiting to see whether the midterms have produced ‌a lasting shift in Trump's approach to the conflict, or whether this is just another temporary change in tone.
The global oil market is showing signs of a return to excess supply as demand drops because of high prices, some analysts say. JP Morgan in a report last week estimated a global oil surplus of 1.4 million barrels per day ​in October.

articles.title_orig: No deal on Ukraine aid? Then no deal on EU budget, Merz says
articles.title_zh: No deal on Ukraine aid? Then no deal on EU budget, Merz says
articles.content_orig:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has made the deal on the European Union's next budget conditional on fresh support for Ukraine, bringing together two politically sensitive topics that have exposed deep divisions among member states.
Kyiv is staring down a €70 billion shortfall in its 2027 budget caused by Russia's relentless airstrikes. The EU has promised to cover two-thirds of this gap, roughly €45 billion, through a yet-to-be-defined instrument.
"A collective commitment that all of us, without exception, will contribute fairly to closing this gap is an essential prerequisite for resolving this issue and for discussing any further matters, particularly those with financial implications," Merz said in a letter addressed to European Council President António Costa and seen by Euronews.
Merz argued that the ongoing negotiations on the bloc's seven-year budget should guarantee "a solution supported by all member states that ensures a sound and multiannual financing perspective for Ukraine from 2028 onwards, including the interest liabilities that have already accrued".
The interest refers to the ongoing €90 billion support loan, which is backed by common borrowing among 24 countries. Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic secured an opt-out from the credit line in exchange for providing the necessary unanimity.
The principal will not be repaid until Russia agrees to war reparations. However, interest payments will start falling due next year. Initially, Brussels estimated €3 billion per year, but the steep rise in borrowing costs has altered the calculation.
The €45 billion that the EU intends to provide Kyiv in 2027 will come on top of the existing loan.
Given the massive scale of the gap, a new round of joint debt has quickly emerged as the frontrunner option. The European Commission is set to present countries with possible options ahead of a special summit at the end of the month.
In the letter, Merz asks Costa to accelerate the timeline for discussions by putting the matter as a "priority" at this week's informal summit in Dublin. The topic was not originally foreseen in the agenda.
The chancellor pointedly regrets that financial and military support for the war-weary country is "distributed unevenly and carried mostly by only a few member states".
"Supporting Ukraine is a matter of our indivisible European security, and so must be the burden sharing for that support," he writes.
Germany is the largest bilateral donor to Ukraine. Other key backers, such as Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden, share Merz's grievances and want to merge the budget and Ukraine into one single package.
All these countries happen to belong to the so-called "frugals" or "modernisers" who advocate across-the-board cuts to the draft budget. This has put them on a collision course with the "Friends of Cohesion", who are fighting to retain a high level of expenditure.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia are signalling they will once again exempt themselves from joint debt to support Kyiv. Bulgaria, a vocal critic of weapons deliveries, is expected to follow suit. The four sit in the cohesion group.
Their refusal to participate has angered the so-called “frugal” countries.
"The cohesion camp cannot have their cake and eat it," a diplomat said. "There is no money tree in Brussels, so we need to make political choices."
Simon Harris, Ireland's finance minister, whose country holds the rotating presidency and moderates negotiations, sided with the "frugals".
"It's very hard to have a serious conversation about the European budget for the next several years without Ukraine and the financing of Ukraine," Harris said on Monday morning before heading into a ministerial meeting in Brussels.
"We do need to frame this correctly. This is actually European security."
But not all member states share the same position.
Ignacy Niemczycki, Poland's deputy minister in charge of European affairs, argued last week that the two issues are fundamentally distinct and binding them together could "backfire" and make a final deal "even more difficult" than it is now.
Meanwhile, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico warned that such a link would be "very dangerous".

articles.title_orig: Sony’s new PlayStation Portal handheld includes ‘additional’ internal storage
articles.title_zh: Sony’s new PlayStation Portal handheld includes ‘additional’ internal storage
articles.content_orig:
The Japan-only model arrives on December 10th in a midnight black color scheme.
The Japan-only model arrives on December 10th in a midnight black color scheme.
Sony is launching a new version of its PlayStation Portal exclusively in Japan next month. The updated model will launch in the midnight black color option we’ve seen before , and will include “additional” internal storage for future-looking features.
It’s the additional internal storage that’s the surprise change to this particular model, which will be locked to Japanese language options and can only be used with a PlayStation account registered in Japan. Sony says the extra storage is for “future functionality” that it will announce once these features are finalized.
Sony is also renaming this particular Portal from PlayStation Portal Remote Player to PlayStation Portal Player. The name change, combined with extra internal storage, seems to suggest that this particular model might get access to streaming apps.
The existing PlayStation Portal doesn’t support streaming apps like YouTube, Disney Plus, or Netflix, and is primarily designed to stream PS5 games from a console or the cloud. The PlayStation Portal isn’t powerful enough to play PlayStation games locally, but extra storage could also let you sync media for offline playback.
This Japan-only PlayStation Portal is launching on December 10th, priced at 39,980 yen (around $253).

articles.title_orig: Palestinian Authority land freeze targets Arab Israelis after Jewish home purchases near Jericho
articles.title_zh: Palestinian Authority land freeze targets Arab Israelis after Jewish home purchases near Jericho
articles.content_orig:
The Palestinian Authority temporarily suspended land registration transactions last week for people holding Israeli citizenship or Jerusalem residency, following the purchase of eight homes by Jewish activists near Jericho, a city in Area A, according to an official announcement by the Palestinian Land Authority.
Lt.-Col. (res.) Maurice Hirsch, director of the Initiative for Palestinian Authority Accountability and Reform at the Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs, argued that the PA likely believed the Israeli Jews had acquired the homes with the assistance of Israeli Arabs.
Palestinian law treats the sale or lease of land to Israeli Jews as an act of treason, which can carry severe penalties, including life imprisonment with hard labor and potentially the death penalty. In 2019, a Nablus court sentenced a Palestinian man to five years in prison for allegedly attempting to sell land to Israeli Jews. In 2018, a Kalkilya court sentenced two Palestinian men to 15 years of hard labor for their involvement in a network seeking to transfer West Bank land to Israeli Jews.
“The decision exposes a fundamental contradiction in Palestinian Authority policy. While the PA considers Arab citizens and residents of Israel to be Palestinians, it now treats their Israeli citizenship as grounds for restricting their property transactions,” Hirsch wrote in a publication for the JCPA.
He added: “The PA’s latest restrictions on Israeli Arab property transactions represent another dimension of this policy, extending its consequences beyond Palestinians living under PA jurisdiction to Arab citizens and residents of Israel.”
The PA has long regarded the approximately two million Arab citizens of Israel as Palestinian, regardless of their integration into Israeli society, military service, or self-described identities. However, the latest suspension, though a temporary restriction that has now been lifted, introduced one of the first distinctions based on the Israeli citizenship and residency status of Arabs.
Despite the Oslo Accords excluding Israeli citizens from the PA’s personal jurisdiction, the PA has attempted to prosecute Israeli Arabs in the past for their alleged roles in land transfers to Jews and other alleged crimes.
The location of the eight homes is also significant. Although Jericho is in Area A, under PA civil and security control, the properties in question are located in Area C, which is under full Israeli civil and security control. Under the Oslo Accords, the PA’s territorial jurisdiction does not extend to Area C, and Israeli citizens are also excluded from its personal jurisdiction. This raises questions about the PA’s authority to investigate or prosecute Israeli citizens in connection with the purchases, even if Israeli Arabs were involved in facilitating the transactions.

articles.title_orig: Honda to invest $3 billion in new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio
articles.title_zh: Honda to invest $3 billion in new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio
articles.content_orig:
MARYSVILLE, Ohio — Honda Motor plans to invest $3 billion to build a new vehicle assembly plant in Ohio, the automaker announced Monday.
Honda said the new plant, which will be near its other facilities in Marysville, Ohio, is expected to begin production in 2029, have a capacity for 240,000 vehicles annually and create more than 2,000 jobs.
The facility is expected to be capable of producing traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines, all-electric vehicles and hybrid models, which have been growing in popularity in the U.S.
The plant is expected to increase Honda's light-duty vehicle capacity to 1.3 million units annually in the U.S. It currently has 12 manufacturing plants in United States, eight of which produce engines or light-duty vehicles for the auto industry.
It's the company's first new mass production U.S. vehicle assembly plant since it opened a facility in Indiana in 2008. It also opened a $70 million performance vehicle facility in 2016 and a multibillion-dollar joint venture battery plant earlier this year, both in Ohio.
"This is not simply an investment in another plant. It is an investment in the future of Honda manufacturing in America," Bob Nelson, executive vice president of American Honda Motor, said during the announcement at the company's U.S. heritage center in Ohio.
The auto industry has been trying to localize more production amid President Donald Trump 's tariffs and inflated logistics costs that have cut into profits.
Honda's plans for a new plant come roughly two weeks after Volkswagen-owned luxury brand Audi announced it would invest more than $4 billion in its first U.S. manufacturing facility in Georgia.
Detroit automakers General Motors and Ford Motor and international automakers Toyota Motor and Hyundai Motor also recently said they will spend billions of dollars on new or updated U.S. facilities.
Honda's announcement comes after the automaker in May indefinitely suspended an $11 billion investment plan to produce all-electric vehicles and batteries in Canada. It also canceled three planned EVs for the U.S. market.
The new Ohio plant is expected to notably boost Honda's U.S. production and American-produced sales. Honda said nearly all of its vehicles sold in the U.S., including its Acura luxury brand, were produced in North America, including more than 60% in the U.S.
American Honda Motor Co. executive Jennifer Thomas recently emphasized the Japanese automaker's commitment to the U.S. and need for additional capacity.
"In order to be competitive in this market, you're going to need to build products here," Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs, said Oct. 27 in Detroit. "We are focused on trying to maximize the existing capacity that we have, but we are at capacity, and so we're exploring all options."
Thomas also warned the automotive industry faces a "catastrophic" scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, when Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don't reach a deal.
Honda said it has built more than 33 million vehicles and more than 39 million engines in the U.S. since it started auto production in the U.S. in 1982.
The Japanese automaker currently has more than 30,000 employees in the U.S.

articles.title_orig: Syria Signs Deal With China for 6.5 Million Prepaid Electricity Meters, Raising Questions Over Consumer Costs
articles.title_zh: Syria Signs Deal With China for 6.5 Million Prepaid Electricity Meters, Raising Questions Over Consumer Costs
articles.content_orig:
[DAMASCUS] The Syrian Electricity Company signed an agreement with Chinese company Wasion Group Limited on Sunday to supply 6.5 million prepaid smart electricity meters, as part of efforts to modernize electricity consumption monitoring and improve power grid management in Syria. The deal raises questions about its cost, financing arrangements, and potential impact on consumers’ electricity bills.
The agreement was signed at the Syrian Electricity Company’s headquarters in Damascus, in the presence of representatives from both the Syrian and Chinese sides, as part of a broader government plan to modernize the energy sector and introduce digital systems into electricity services.
The media office of the Syrian Electricity Company, which operates under the Ministry of Energy, told The Media Line that the agreement includes the supply of 6 million single-phase meters, primarily intended for residential properties and small businesses, along with 500,000 three-phase meters, typically used by commercial and industrial facilities requiring greater electrical capacity.
According to the media office, the agreement also includes software systems and technical equipment necessary to operate the meters, allowing for more accurate consumption measurements, improved customer data management, reduced electricity losses, and more efficient network monitoring.
The media office explained that the prepaid metering system requires consumers to purchase electricity credit before using power, rather than paying periodic bills based on consumption recorded after use.
The new system is expected to improve electricity bill collection, reduce errors associated with traditional meter readings, and enable subscribers to monitor their electricity consumption more accurately.

The official announcement did not disclose the financial value of the contract or specify who would bear the costs of purchasing and installing the meters. It also did not clarify whether subscribers would be required to pay fees to replace their existing meters or how the prepaid system would be implemented for low-income households.
Authorities have also not announced a specific timetable for delivering all the meters covered by the agreement or identified which governorates will be included in the initial phase of implementation.
Khaled Abu Di, director of the General Establishment for Electricity Transmission and Distribution, previously announced that the institution had developed a plan to replace conventional electricity meters with smart meters over approximately three years.
In January 2026, Abu Di revealed that around 1.2 million electricity subscribers in Syria still lacked electricity meters, highlighting the scale of the challenges involved in modernizing metering, billing, and revenue collection systems.
The agreement comes as Syria’s electricity sector continues to face significant challenges following years of war, including damage to power generation facilities and transmission and distribution networks, as well as the need for substantial investment to rehabilitate infrastructure and improve the reliability of electricity supplies.
Although introducing smart meters could improve consumption management and reduce commercial electricity losses, modernizing metering systems does not necessarily mean an increase in electricity generation or an end to power outages. Improving the number of hours electricity is available also requires upgrading power plants, transmission and distribution networks, and securing reliable energy supplies.
The prepaid nature of the new meters raises additional questions about their impact on Syrian households, particularly amid difficult economic conditions and concerns about consumers’ ability to regularly purchase electricity credit.
It also remains unclear whether the government intends to introduce changes to electricity tariffs alongside the new system or will limit the initiative to modernizing metering and payment collection procedures.
The agreement represents another step in economic and technological cooperation between Syria and China, as Damascus seeks to attract foreign companies to participate in rehabilitating public services and infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention
articles.title_zh: Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention
articles.content_orig:
An inquiry from the U.S. Commerce Dept. into Singapore data center Megaspeed was transferred to the Department of Justice after Nvidia NVDA intervened, The New York Times reported.
Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter reached out for information to the Commerce Dept., according to the news outlet. Teter did so after Nvidia received permission from Jeff Kessler, a top official at the Commerce Department. Kessler reports directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.
The inquiry into Megaspeed was then transferred to the DOJ to avoid a potential compromise into the investigation, the news outlet added, citing people familiar with the matter. The DOJ is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed, people familiar with the matter told the news outlet.
The Commerce Dept. did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Seeking Alpha.
An Nvidia spokesperson said the company regularly speaks to government agencies "to answer their questions, provide information we have gathered from the field, request their guidance and instructions, and ask whether they have any follow-ups."
"When we have requests from customers for new shipments, service, or support, we have an obligation to resolve any potential 'red flags' before proceeding," the spokesperson told Seeking Alpha. "That process can include asking BIS, OEE, or other government agencies whether they require any further information from us. We work to resolve any allegations of 'diversion' promptly, to help government and our partners halt any would-be smugglers while serving the critical market of lawful customers that help America win worldwide. Unresolved questions about lawful business undercut longstanding U.S. policy and hurt American economic and national security."
Over the weekend, Nvidia's board of directors disclosed that it opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang on the prospect of potentially being targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. Separately, Huang disclosed that he had been unfaithful to his wife in conjunction with the matter with Alice Huang (no relation), a Singapore-based data center executive.
Ms. Huang, who also goes by Huang Le, is alleged to have spied on the Nvidia founder. U.S. officials have been investigating Huang and Megaspeed since 2024.
Nvidia shares fell 4.5% in late morning trading amid investor scrutiny following the disclosure.
A number of Wall Street firms weighed in on the matter, including Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives, one of Nvidia's biggest bulls on Wall Street.
“Jensen has become the global face of the AI Revolution and that now will be front and center for Nvidia how to navigate this very difficult situation looking forward,” Ives wrote in a note to clients. “This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons.”

articles.title_orig: Ukraine’s Drone Pilots Turn to Israeli-Italian Comms to Replace Musk’s SpaceX
articles.title_zh: Ukraine’s Drone Pilots Turn to Israeli-Italian Comms to Replace Musk’s SpaceX
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Ukraine may be adopting Israeli-Italian HiSKY satellite links for deep-strike drones, trading Starlink’s capacity in exchange for greater resistance to jamming and US interference. Use remains unconfirmed, but recent refinery strikes suggest improved accuracy and effectiveness.
Ukraine’s long-range drone forces are shifting away from higher capacity but politically unreliable satellite communications delivered by Elon Musk’s SpaceX satellite network to data links using Israeli-Italian technology that is a lot less capable but impossible for the White House to shut off, Russian and Ukrainian news reports said on Sunday.
Claims first appearing in late October in Russian military media said the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) had started installing aboard drones targeting oil refineries and military infrastructure deep inside Russia terminals that access the HiSKY SmartLight satellite communications system, an alternative to the US-manufactured Starlink or Starshield receivers that had been in near-universal AFU use since 2022.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Russian military analyst Konstantin Malofeev in an Oct. 30 report said that a HiSKY-equipped drone operating over Russia is unjammable because the system automatically hops from commercial satellite to commercial satellite if the signal degrades. The Ukrainian shift away from SpaceX’s Starlink system was driven by a Musk decision to block Ukrainian use of Starlink coverage over Russia “because otherwise Russia would shoot down Musk’s satellites,” he said.
The shift to HiSKY helped Ukrainian drone operators make unimpeded swarm attacks against Russian oil refineries and to pilot multiple aircraft to single out and hit vulnerable locations of the plants, Malofeev said.
The Russia-associated Coordination Center for the Assistance of New Russia (CCANR), in an Oct. 29 analytical video published on RuTube, said that authorities had obtained “confirmed information” that Ukraine’s drone forces had begun using HiSKY technology in attacks on Russia:
“This is not Starlink. This is European equipment that allows, using European communications networks, the piloting of long-range drones and other devices, like crewless boats, against the entire territory of the Russian Federation,” said CCANR Director Aleksandr Liubimov. “There are no limitations to the capacities of this equipment like there are on Starlink, which doesn’t work in Russia.”
“According to our information [the Ukrainians] are testing this technology in border regions of Russia with the objective of using it more widely,” Liubimov said . “We [Russia] can expect mass use of drones [equipped with HiSKY terminals] against any point in the Russian Federation using this space communications system, specifically that does not belong to [SpaceX CEO Elon] Musk, but to Europe.”
HiSKY, according to corporate-published information, is an Israeli company with a British subsidiary, hiSkySat Ltd., operating an R&D center at Harwell in Oxfordshire. The UK Space Agency is funding the project with £9 million ($12 million) allocated through the European Space Agency (ESA), a UK government statement said.
Serhiy “Flash” Beskresnikov, a Ukrainian military communications expert and advisor to President Volodymyr Zelensky on military electronics, in Sunday comments to Euromaidan Press said: “I do not confirm or deny this information from the Russians. I do not know why this caused such a stir in Russian media since such technologies have long been nothing unique.”
Companies owned by the world’s richest individual, Musk, on or about Oct. 14 imposed a slowdown on SpaceX-associated terminals operated in Ukraine, so that if the terminal moved at more than 160 kph (100 mph) its communications would stop working. The degradation effectively made Ukrainian strikes by Starlink- and Starshield-equipped aircraft impossible, and at the same time made high-speed Ukrainian-developed interceptor drones used by the AFU against Russian jet-propelled drones useless.
Musk said the White House ordered SpaceX to impose the speed cap while White House officials said it was Musk’s idea. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky blamed his US counterpart, Donald Trump. According to Zelensky and other Ukrainian officials, dozens of million-dollar drones en route to Russia fell out of the sky the first day the slowdown went into effect.
Sharp international reaction to the US attack on Ukrainian drone strike capacity, along with a congressional order to SpaceX to submit to a formal congressional investigation about the speed limit with hearings starting in January, helped restore Starlink and Starshield service to AFU units by Oct. 24.
The AFU, according to Ukrainian media reports, began employing HiSKY’s smallest and lowest-cost terminal, a 6-kilogram (13-pound) device called a Sirius 16x16 Ku, in drone strikes against Russia in mid-October while the Musk/White House-imposed limits to SpaceX-provided service still were in effect. The first debris of a Ukrainian HiSKY-equipped drone was shot down by Russian air defense forces shortly before the end of the month, those reports said.
According to a Sunday article by the Ukrainian research group DP Defpulse , AFU use of HiSKY technology is not fully confirmed but highly probable. The system gives AFU operators the advantage of communications links transferring 2 Mbps of data in concentrated beams that hop from high-orbit geostationary satellite to geostationary satellite as needed, making the electronic tether between drone and operator almost impossible to jam, the report said.
The main disadvantage to Ukrainian pilots is that Starlink or Starshield terminals using the SpaceX network and a massive constellation of moving, low orbit satellites offer 50-250+ Mbps data transfer capacity, making piloting a long-range drone visually possible only via Starlink, because data transfer volume using HiSKY technology is too limited. A lower-volume HiSKY link would nonetheless be capable of transferring course corrections to a drone in flight, making possible redirection of individual drones in a drone strike package to a precise target, the report said.
From Oct. 15 to Oct. 29, Ukraine paused its oil refinery strikes against Russia following a US request to do so and White House threats that the US might retaliate against Ukraine if Ukraine kept on attacking Russia’s energy sector, which, according to the White House, was driving up prices at the pump for US motorists.
Overnight on Oct. 30-Nov. 1, Ukraine seemingly defied the US with a new wave of drone attacks against Russian oil refineries.
Among the facilities attacked were the Novokuibyshevsk refinery in Samara Oblast (Oct. 30), the Kstovo refinery in Nizhniy Novogorod Oblast (Nov. 1), the Samara oil dispatch station (Nov. 2), Yaroslavl’s Yanos refinery (Nov. 3), the Ryazan oil refinery (Nov. 5), Krasnodar’s Afipsky oil refinery (Nov. 6), a second Saratov refinery (Nov. 7) and St. Petersburg’s KINEF refinery near the village Kirishi overnight Sunday-Monday.
According to reports in local media and overhead satellite imagery recorded by the US worldwide fire watch agency FIRMS , the Ukrainian strike packages hitting Nizhniy Novogorod, Yaroslavl and Ryazan were more accurate than strikes in past months, with aircraft concentrating on distillation towers and cracking equipment, and setting multiple fires that sometimes burned for days. On Monday afternoon, some 12 hours after the Ukrainian attack, more than two-thirds of the KINEF refinery was still in flames, FIRMS data showed.
